name: oe-kimi-F-S-P
finalResponse:
Before the plan, a word about the story this company is telling itself — because the story may be the real constraint. The narrative is "we tried speed once, and it cost us two years of warranty pain." That's a lesson, but possibly the wrong one. What the last attempt likely proved is that *pressure* is dangerous — expediting, overloading inspectors, rushing assembly. It said nothing about what happens when you remove waiting instead. Those are very different kinds of speed, and conflating them means the organization is fighting the last war.

Two other assumptions worth holding loosely: is 14 weeks the measured flow time or the quoted number? Quotes get padded by everyone who doesn't trust the system, and padding is a different disease than slowness. And what does the competitor's 6 weeks actually consist of — the same certification regime and customization, or a stocked module with a data book attached? You may not need to do your process faster. You may need to sell a different architecture of product.

With that, some threads to pull:

**Follow one order home before launching anything.** Resist the urge to announce a lead-time reduction program — programs trigger the immune system, and this organization's immune system remembers the warranty spike vividly. Instead, have two or three trusted people quietly walk a few recent orders, calendar in hand, recording when work actually touched the product versus when it sat. I'd wager the touch time measures in days. The weeks will be found in queue: order engineering before release, materials ordered only after contract signature, batches waiting for inspection slots, documentation chased at the end. This investigation doesn't need a mandate or a budget. It needs someone who asks good questions and doesn't file a report too soon.

**Make the product wait less, not the people work faster.** This is the reframe that protects quality. The gates don't have to move at all if the queues in front of them disappear. Concretely: standardize an option catalog so most orders become configure-to-order rather than engineer-to-order; run order engineering in parallel with commercial close instead of after it; shrink batch sizes so parts stop waiting for their siblings. None of this touches a single inspection. It just stops the product from sitting.

**Inventory is stored time.** Long-lead items — castings, certified materials with mill certs, specialized components — are probably being purchased sequentially, after the order lands, out of habit rather than necessity. Blanket orders against forecast, with certificates arriving *with* the material rather than chased afterward, can take weeks out without the factory changing anything. And if the competitor is quoting 6 weeks, they are almost certainly starting from a shelf of semi-finished standard modules and configuring late. Postponement is worth a long look: build the common core to stock, customize at the end.

**Schedule around the true constraint, and quote from the real load.** Somewhere there is an actual bottleneck — the test cell, the certified inspectors, final assembly. Find it, protect it, subordinate everything else to its calendar. Then consider something sales may find uncomfortable: quote lead time dynamically from actual backlog rather than as a fixed padded number. A live quote is honest in a way a blanket 14 never is, and it converts lead time from a promise into a signal. A fast lane for high-runner standard configurations — reserved capacity slots — lets you compete at 6 weeks where it matters most, before the whole system is ready.

**Keep every gate. Change what the gate waits for.** The inspection itself takes hours; the queue for the inspector takes weeks. Embed certified inspection capability into the flow — in-process verification by qualified people at the point of work — rather than treating inspection as an event the line halts for. And here's a question few companies ask: when did anyone last talk to the certification body about what's actually required versus what's simply always been done? Many regimes permit delegated source inspection, witness points instead of hold points, manufacturer sign-off under periodic audit. The gates may be more negotiable than habit suggests. Change nothing without capability evidence first, and instrument the transition honestly — first-pass yield at each gate, rework hours, and early-life warranty telemetry with a defined tripwire. That telemetry is also your political protection: when someone invokes the last failure, you want data, not defensiveness.

Which raises a question worth answering before any of this: what *actually* failed last time? Which stage, which failure mode, which shortcut? That diagnosis is a map of exactly what to protect — and it may reveal that the spike came from two or three specific pressure points, not from speed itself.

**The feud is a measurement artifact, not a personality problem.** Sales is paid on bookings, production on efficiency, quality on zero escapes — each locally rational, collectively slow. Blame thrives in separate scoreboards. Rather than a collaboration initiative (which nobody believes in anyway), give them one number to share: order-to-ship calendar time, jointly owned. Then have the three functions walk one order's journey together, weekly, standing where the work sits. It's hard to blame another department when you're both watching the same crate wait nine days for an inspection slot. And recognize that this is a trade, not a surrender: if sales wants speed, it gives something — forecast discipline, spec stability after release, a restricted options menu on fast-lane products. Worth asking whether sales wants speed badly enough to pay for it. One in three deals lost on delivery is a striking number; sometimes "delivery" is the reason customers give when the real one is price. It would be useful to know which.

Pilot all of this on one product family — the one with the most repeat demand — and let the result argue for itself. A quiet 9-week reality on one line will do more than any announcement.

A few things I'd want to know before committing to any of it: Is leadership prepared to discover that most of the 14 weeks is self-inflicted — padding, queues, habit? That finding implicates everyone a little, and certain people's metrics specifically, and organizations have been known to prefer the feud to the finding. And who already knows where the time goes? The expediters, the schedulers, the senior inspectors — the people who work around the system daily — usually have the map in their heads. They rarely volunteer it to a program. They'll often tell it to one person who asks well.

Find them first. The plan is mostly already written — it's just distributed across people nobody's asked.
